gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2's solar input takes only 8.2 A at 11–28 V but 14.5 A at 29–60 V. Anker's own 200 W panel in the kit outputs 48 V ⎓ 4.16 A, so it sits in the high-current band, while any panel whose operating voltage is 28 V or less is held to 8.2 A × Vmp. On this model, that limit can cancel out the cheaper-third-party-panel route.
standout_why: I read the cited rivals and our own page. stormwatts.com (bundle math) gives only wattage caps (AC180 500 W, Explorer 1000 v2 400 W): no voltage bands, current limits or connectors. getwattlogic.com says inputs are 'MC4 or XT60' without saying which station uses which, and gives no voltage, current or watt limits. trek4tech.com (top uncited result) gives the C1000 Gen 2 '600W' and a general '11–60V' window but not the current split by voltage. Dealectric's current page pairs the AC180 with a $210 third-party 200 W panel without checking it against the AC180's 10 A cap. None of the pages gives a per-model current limit. I rate it 2 rather than 3 because I couldn't open a specific third-party panel's Vmp/Imp to put a sourced number on the loss.
decides: For the Anker C1000 Gen 2, the kit already saves nothing ($1,199.99 vs $1,199.98 on our page), and buying separately with a low-voltage 200 W folding panel adds a power penalty. For example, a panel with Vmp 20 V is capped at 8.2 A × 20 V = 164 W on this station. Anker's 48 V PS200 avoids the cap. So for this model, buy Anker's matched panel (as a kit or separately) or a high-voltage third-party panel, not a cheap low-voltage one. For the AC180, the 10 A / 12–60 V Voc limits mean a third-party panel needs Imp of 10 A or less to deliver its full rating. Our page's $659 AC180 + third-party-panel pairing should be checked against that before we recommend it. A related price fix for angle A: BLUETTI's AC180 + 200W Solar variant was $769 today, not $729, and the AC180 showed as in stock.
